assessment.nobel_worthiness: A foundational body of experimental and theoretical work that established social preferences as central to economic behavior and institutions.
assessment.attribution: The proposed trio captures complementary evidence, theory, and mechanisms concerning reciprocity, fairness, and inequity aversion.
assessment.maturity: The contribution has shaped several decades of research and is tested across laboratory, field, and applied settings.
uncertainties: The appropriate division of credit among the wider social-preferences literature remains contestable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Audit and correspondence designs made discrimination measurable in consequential labor-market settings and transformed empirical work on unequal treatment.
assessment.attribution: Bertrand and Mullainathan are especially closely associated with a landmark modern audit design, while Charles represents the broader program.
assessment.maturity: The designs have been extensively replicated, adapted, and incorporated into policy-relevant empirical research.
uncertainties: Audit estimates identify discrimination within specific hiring stages and settings rather than every mechanism generating labor-market inequality.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population administrative-data research substantially changed measurement and understanding of intergenerational mobility and its geographic variation.
assessment.attribution: Chetty, Hendren, and Friedman form a coherent core for the linked empirical program.
assessment.maturity: The research has generated a large follow-on literature and has durable implications for education, housing, and public policy.
uncertainties: Interpretation of place effects and the mechanisms behind mobility remains actively debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work clarified how early-life health and environments shape human-capital accumulation and later economic outcomes.
assessment.attribution: The proposed recipients represent complementary empirical evidence and dynamic models of skill formation.
assessment.maturity: The early-life perspective is well established, influential across economics, and supported by a broad body of evidence.
uncertainties: The relative contribution of particular interventions versus correlated family and environmental conditions is difficult to isolate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic discrete-choice methods supplied a practical framework for estimating forward-looking behavior and transformed structural empirical economics.
assessment.attribution: Rust is the clearest central innovator, with Keane and Eckstein important developers and appliers of the framework.
assessment.maturity: The methods have had long-lasting use in labor, industrial organization, transport, and public economics.
uncertainties: Structural conclusions can depend materially on modeling assumptions and computational choices.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The combination of theory and empirical measurement made adverse selection in insurance markets tractable and policy relevant.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein, Einav, and Salanie provide a coherent set of theoretical and empirical contributors to the modern literature.
assessment.maturity: The framework has been widely used across insurance markets and has informed evaluation of insurance design.
uncertainties: Empirical separation of selection, moral hazard, and market design remains context dependent.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collective household models replaced the unitary-household assumption with a productive account of bargaining, allocation, and distribution within families.
assessment.attribution: Chiappori, Lundberg, and Pollak are central contributors to the theoretical and empirical development of the collective approach.
assessment.maturity: The framework is longstanding and influential in family, labor, development, and public economics.
uncertainties: Empirical identification of bargaining power and distribution factors can be demanding.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification established a disciplined way to draw credible conclusions when standard point-identifying assumptions are unavailable.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the foundational figure, with Tamer and Molinari making major contributions to moment-inequality methods and implementation.
assessment.maturity: The approach is theoretically mature and increasingly important wherever transparent assumptions and robust inference are essential.
uncertainties: Its policy influence is less immediately visible than that of some applied empirical programs.
